```{python}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
import json, os, sys
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
ROOT = Path.cwd()
while not (ROOT / "config" / "project.yaml").exists():
    ROOT = ROOT.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT)); os.chdir(ROOT)
def handoff(a):
    p = ROOT / "context" / "handoffs" / f"{a}.json"
    return json.loads(p.read_text()) if p.exists() else {}
```

# Why this page exists

This site is the output of an experiment in which **sixteen separate AI agents** designed, built,
calibrated and evaluated hydrological models for one watershed, coordinating only through files on disk.

The sections that follow explain the brief that started it, the vocabulary needed to read the rest of the
site (*agent*, *orchestration*, *skill*, *context*, *handoff*), the guardrails that make the result
trustworthy, and an honest account of what went wrong along the way. Read this first; the per-agent
reports in the sidebar assume it.

# The original brief {#sec-prompt}

The project began with a single instruction from the user. It is reproduced verbatim, because everything
downstream is either a direct consequence of it or a documented deviation from it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## The prompt, as given

> Create multi-agent orchestration configuration files to model the Leaf River watershed in Mississippi, USA.
>
> Goal: create the best mode that reproduce streamflow accurately
>
> I want the following agents:
>
> **Agent 1:** Characterize the watershed based on available online information.
>
> **Agent 2:** Describe and evaluate the data attached (LeafRiverDaily.txt), creating a Quarto report with an extensive description of the available variables
>
> **Agent 3:** Based on the limited information, propose a set of 5 models to use for this task. Create a Quarto document describing each model in an extensive way, including the conceptual and mathematical framework of each one (should be available in Python, or create them from scratch based on the main processes that could be interesting to represent based on the information provided by agents 1 and 2). The model it could be as basic as a simple linear regression or complex
>
> **Agent 4:** create a list of all the possible metrics that could be useful for this task, in a Quarto document as well, and recommend the one that suits the best for this case
>
> **Agents 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9:** each one in charge of building each model
>
> **Agent 10:** create a list of optimization algorithms (Quarto document) and recommend the best fit for this case
>
> **Agents 11, 12, 13, 14, and 15:** each one in charge of parameter optimization of the above models
>
> **Agent 16:** Evaluate the model and select the best one. For this case, report KGE and NSE metrics.
>
> The evaluation period should follow: Performance metric values should be computed by running the model for the period from Oct 1, 1948 through Sept 30, 1951. The first three months (Oct 1 through Dec 31) of 1948 are used as a "warm-up" period to allow for state initialization errors to be minimized – accordingly, the metric values were computed only for the period from Jan 1, 1949 to Sept 30, 1951.
>
> The previous period could be used as calibration
>
> Create the configuration files to later start working with each agent.
>
> You have total freedom to select the best options for this task. Create backup of the work to provide context to other agents. Create skills for every agent, in a very detailed way.
>
> Ask me anything that it's missing here.
:::

## One thing in the brief could not be taken literally

The brief says the evaluation window is Oct 1 1948 – Sep 30 1951 and that *"the previous period could be
used as calibration"*. **There is no previous period**: the data file begins on 1 October 1948, so the
evaluation window sits at the very start of the record. Calibration therefore had to run *forward* from
1 October 1951 to the end of the record in 1988. This is logged in `context/DECISIONS.md` as a scaffold-time
decision rather than silently assumed.

# The vocabulary {#sec-vocabulary}

## Agent

An **agent** is a language model given (a) a role, (b) a specific set of tools — read files, write files,
run shell commands, search the web — and (c) a task, which it then carries out autonomously: deciding what
to read, what code to write, what to check, and when it is finished.

The important property is that an agent is *not* a script. It makes judgement calls. Several of the most
consequential results in this study came from an agent deciding to do something it was not explicitly told
to do — and several of the problems came from the same freedom.

Each agent here is defined by a short Markdown file in `.claude/agents/`, e.g.:

```yaml
---
name: a06-model-builder-2
description: Implements model slot 2 from config/models.yaml as a tested Python module.
tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep
model: opus
skills: [a06-model-builder-2]
---
```

## Sub-agent and context isolation

Each of the sixteen agents runs as a **sub-agent**: a separate conversation with its own fresh context
window, launched by a coordinating "orchestrator" agent. This matters for a practical reason. A language
model has a finite context; sixteen agents' worth of exploration, dead ends and file dumps would not fit in
one. Isolation means each agent sees only what it needs.

The cost of isolation is that agents cannot talk to each other. Everything they need to share must be
written down — which is what the rest of this machinery is for.

## Orchestration and the dependency graph

**Multi-agent orchestration** is the coordination layer: deciding which agents run, in what order, what
each one needs before it can start, and what it must produce before anything downstream may begin.

Here that graph lives in `orchestration.yaml`. It is a directed acyclic graph grouped into six phases;
agents within a phase are independent and run in parallel.

::: {.column-page}

The phases are not arbitrary. Each one exists because its outputs are *inputs* to the next: you cannot
choose an optimizer (P3) before you know what models you are optimizing (P2) or what objective you are
maximising (P2); you cannot build a model (P4) before its equations are specified (P2).

## Skill

A **skill** is a detailed, reusable procedure attached to an agent — the difference between telling someone
"do the data analysis" and handing them a laboratory protocol. Each agent here has one, in
`.claude/skills/<agent>/SKILL.md`, typically 60–90 lines specifying the exact steps, the statistics to
compute, the figures to produce, the checks that must pass, and the contents of its handoff.

Skills are what make an agent's output *predictable* rather than merely plausible. They also encode
institutional knowledge: a02's skill, for example, mandates a Mann–Kendall trend test, a Pettitt change-point
test and a double-mass curve — quality checks a general instruction would not have produced.

## Context, handoffs, and shared memory

Because agents cannot speak to one another, the project uses a set of append-only files as shared memory:

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `context/CONTEXT.md` | Each agent appends one section on finishing: key findings with units, outputs, what downstream agents must know. |
| `context/handoffs/aNN.json` | Machine-readable results: `key_numbers`, `assumptions`, `downstream_notes` addressed to specific later agents. |
| `context/DECISIONS.md` | Every non-obvious choice, with the alternatives considered and the reason. |
| `context/ISSUES.md` | Problems found in *other* agents' work. Agents never edit each other's files; they file an issue. |
| `context/state.json` | Which agents are `pending` / `running` / `done`. Gates the whole graph. |
| `context/backups/` + git tags | Every agent commits and tags on finishing, so any step can be rolled back. |

The `downstream_notes` field deserves emphasis: it lets an agent write a message addressed to a specific
future agent that does not exist yet. a01 left a02 a note about unit conversion; a02 left the ML builders
the exact scaling constants they were permitted to use.

# The guardrails {#sec-guardrails}

A multi-agent study can fail silently. Sixteen agents each making a small, locally reasonable choice can
collectively produce a result that is worthless. Four mechanisms were used to prevent that.

**1. One way to load data, one way to score.** Every agent reads the record through
`src/common/data.py` and computes KGE/NSE through `src/common/metrics.py`. Nobody re-implements either. The
canonical metrics file was verified byte-identical to its original at the end of the study.

**2. A hard guard on the held-out window.** The evaluation period is not merely *discouraged* — it is
unreachable. `slice_run(df, "evaluation")` raises `PermissionError` unless the environment variable
`LR_AGENT=a16` is set, and only the evaluator sets it:

```python
def _guard(which, allow_evaluation):
    if which == "evaluation" and not (allow_evaluation and os.environ.get("LR_AGENT") == "a16"):
        raise PermissionError("Evaluation period is reserved for Agent 16 (set LR_AGENT=a16).")
```

This was checked at the end rather than trusted: the guard fires, no model or optimizer code hard-codes
evaluation dates or row indices, and every other agent's code only ever *removes* that variable.

**3. A model contract.** Every model subclasses `BaseModel` with the same `simulate(forcing, params)`
signature, units of mm/day, and determinism given parameters and seed. This is why one shared calibration
runner could drive five structurally unrelated models, and why the evaluator could treat them uniformly.

**4. Pre-registration.** Eight falsifiable hypotheses were written down in [the hypotheses section](03_models.qmd#sec-hypotheses) of the model
report *before* any model was calibrated, so the final report adjudicates predictions rather than
constructing a story around whatever happened.

# What actually happened {#sec-what-happened}

An honest account, because the failures are more instructive than the successes.

## Things the agents caught that a script would not have

- **a01 proved the data file's identity.** Asked only to characterize the watershed, it went further and
  matched the `Q` column against the USGS record for gauge 02472000: **r = 1.000000** over 13,515 days. That
  turned an ambiguity about the calendar into a measurement.
- **a02 measured the units instead of assuming them.** It found `Q` quantised at 0.0012544 mm/day — exactly
  1 ft³/s over 1,950 km² — confirming both the units and the basin area independently.
- **a03 overrode its own instructions.** Told to propose five models, it rejected HYMOD (a default choice)
  because HYMOD's single *linear* store contradicts the non-linear recession a02 had measured, and
  substituted HBV-light with an argument.
- **a08 chose provable correctness over fidelity.** Implementing SAC-SMA, it dropped a line from the
  original Fortran that destroys mass, because keeping it would have made the conservation invariants
  unprovable. It logged the deviation rather than hiding it.

## Things that went wrong

- **The evaluation window was initially wrong.** An early translation of the brief's calendar dates into
  row indices produced rows 265:1360 instead of 0:1095. Both windows contain exactly 1,003 metric days,
  which is why the error was not obvious. It was caught by cross-checking against the user's earlier study
  and confirmed independently by PET seasonality and the USGS match (`ISSUE-001`).
- **Agents collided on shared files.** Running five builders concurrently exposed that `backup.sh` and
  `state.py` were not safe under parallel use — concurrent git commits fight over `index.lock`, and a
  read-modify-write on `state.json` loses siblings' updates. Both were made atomic. Two agents also filed
  *different* issues under the same number, which had to be renumbered.
- **A declared compute budget was never enforced.** `config/optimization.yaml` specified a 90-minute cap
  for the LSTM search, but the runner never read that block: `study.optimize()` was called with no
  `timeout=`. The search ran over seven hours and produced nothing (`ISSUE-006`). It was replaced by a
  budgeted alternative agent that enforces its deadline **in code**, which finished the same experiment in
  7.6 minutes. The lesson is general: *a limit that lives only in a configuration file is not a limit.*

## The headline result contradicted the design

The study was built around a complexity gradient — regression → GR4J → HBV → SAC-SMA → LSTM — to measure
how much complexity buys. On the held-out window the answer was **nothing**: the 26-coefficient ridge
regression achieved the highest NSE of any candidate, and the rank correlation between number of fitted
quantities and KGE across the five models was **−0.70**.

Because the hypothesis was pre-registered, that is reported as a falsification rather than quietly
reframed. [The H1-risk section](03_models.qmd#sec-h1-risk) of the model report was written *after the models were built but before the held-out
window was opened*, specifically so the inconvenient evidence could not be presented as though it had been
expected all along.

# Reading order {#sec-reading-order}

| # | Report | What it establishes |
|---|---|---|
| 01 | [Watershed](01_watershed.qmd) | Where this basin is, how it behaves, what a good model must represent |
| 02 | [Data](02_data.qmd) | What the record contains, whether it can be trusted, what the periods really are |
| 03 | [Models](03_models.qmd) | The five candidates, their equations, and the pre-registered hypotheses |
| 04 | [Metrics](04_metrics.qmd) | Why the calibration objective is 0.5·KGE + 0.5·NSE |
| 05 | [Implementation & calibration](05_implementation.qmd) | How the models were built, tested and fitted |
| 10 | [Optimization](10_optimization.qmd) | Which search algorithm each model gets, and why |
| 16 | [Evaluation](16_evaluation.qmd) | The held-out result, the winner, and the hypothesis verdicts |

# Reproducing this {#sec-repro}

```bash
bash scripts/setup_env.sh          # conda env `leafriver`
conda activate leafriver
python -m pytest -q tests          # 276 tests
python -m src.optimization.runner --slot 2 --seeds 42-51 --stage final
quarto render reports              # this site
```

Everything is seeded (42), every period comes from `config/project.yaml`, and every agent's work is
recoverable from a git tag listed in its handoff.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-runlog
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Every agent that ran, with the backup tag its work is recoverable from."
rows = []
names = {"a01":"watershed characterization","a02":"data EDA & QC","a03":"model proposals",
         "a04":"metrics & objective","a05":"slot 1 build","a06":"slot 2 build","a07":"slot 3 build",
         "a08":"slot 4 build","a09":"slot 5 build","a10":"optimization design",
         "a11":"slot 1 calibration","a12":"slot 2 calibration","a13":"slot 3 calibration",
         "a14":"slot 4 calibration","a15b":"slot 5 calibration (budgeted)","a16":"held-out evaluation"}
for a, what in names.items():
    h = handoff(a)
    rows.append({"agent": a, "task": what,
                 "status": h.get("status", "—"),
                 "backup tag": (h.get("backup_tag") or "—").replace("backup/", "")})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("agent")
```
